author: A Robot
objectives: Students will identify and name the four chambers of the heart, the four heart valves, and the major vessels entering and leaving the heart
Students will trace the path of blood through the heart's dual circulation, naming each chamber, valve, and vessel in order
Students will distinguish the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit and explain why the right and left sides of the heart serve different circulatory functions

Students will explain why the left ventricle has a substantially thicker myocardium than the right ventricle, relating wall thickness to the pressure required to perfuse the systemic versus pulmonary circuits
Students will describe the function of the atrioventricular and semilunar valves in preventing backflow, and identify which valves separate which chambers or chamber-vessel pairs

modules.description: An introduction to the gross anatomy of the human heart, displaying both exterior and cutaway views to orient students to the four chambers, four valves, and major vessels.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the anatomical orientation of the heart in the body
Recognize the four chambers and distinguish right from left side using anatomical perspective
Locate the major vessels entering and leaving the heart on an intact model

components.text: Right Side (Patient's Right) - Left Side (Patient's Left)

clips.changeMeaning: Scene opens with both heart models displayed side by side at stable positions. The models are oriented anatomically with apex pointing downward, establishing the baseline view for structural orientation.
clips.narration: Welcome to the cardiac anatomy lab. You are looking at two views of the human heart side by side. On your left is an intact heart showing the exterior surface and major blood vessels. On your right is a cutaway heart with the anterior wall removed, revealing the internal chambers and valves. Both hearts are oriented in anatomical position: the apex points downward and slightly to the left, and the atria sit at the top.

clips.changeMeaning: Text label updates to emphasize anatomical perspective. The narration clarifies that the heart's right and left sides are labeled from the patient's own perspective, not the observer's view, which is a critical point of confusion for beginning anatomy students.
clips.narration: Pay close attention: the heart's right and left sides are named from the patient's perspective, not from yours as the observer. This means the right atrium and right ventricle are on the patient's right side, which appears on your left as you face them. This is the standard anatomical convention used in all medical and nursing contexts.

clips.changeMeaning: Both heart models subtly shift to highlight the region where major vessels enter and exit. The vessels are identified in a quick overview before the detailed structural tour begins in the next module.
clips.narration: Before we examine the internal structures, notice the major vessels visible on the intact heart. Blood returns from the body through the superior and inferior vena cava. The pulmonary trunk splits into the pulmonary arteries, which carry blood to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs via the pulmonary veins. The aorta departs the top of the heart to distribute blood throughout the body.

modules.moduleName: Structural Tour: Chambers, Valves, and Vessels
modules.description: A guided walkthrough of each major heart structure, using labels and highlights to connect interior anatomy to exterior landmarks.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Name the four chambers in anatomical order
Identify the four valves and the structures they separate
Locate the five major vessels and their relationship to the chambers

clips.changeMeaning: The cutaway heart model comes into focus as the primary teaching tool. A text label appears above the right atrium. Both the cutaway and intact hearts are subtly highlighted at the right atrium location to establish the connection between interior and exterior views.
clips.narration: Let's begin with the four chambers. The first chamber blood enters is the right atrium, shown here in the upper right portion of the cutaway view. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood returning from the body. Notice how on the intact heart to the left, the right atrium corresponds to this exterior surface region. As we progress through each structure, you'll see both the internal and external anatomy.

clips.changeMeaning: The label moves to highlight the right ventricle, then the left atrium, then the left ventricle in sequence. Each chamber is briefly highlighted with color overlay on both models, showing the spatial relationship between the cutaway view and the intact surface.
clips.narration: Below the right atrium is the right ventricle, which pumps blood to the lungs. Moving to the left side, the left atrium receives oxygenated blood returning from the lungs. Below it is the left ventricle, the most muscular chamber, which pumps blood throughout the entire body. Notice that the left ventricle wall appears thicker than the right—we'll explore why in a later scene.

clips.changeMeaning: The view focuses on the valve regions. Labels highlight the tricuspid valve between the right atrium and ventricle, and the mitral valve between the left atrium and ventricle. A color wash shows the opening between each pair of chambers.
clips.narration: The four valves maintain one-way blood flow. The tricuspid valve sits between the right atrium and right ventricle, allowing blood to flow downward into the ventricle but preventing backflow into the atrium. The mitral valve—also called the bicuspid valve—performs the same role on the left side. Both names are used clinically, so you should be comfortable recognizing both terms.

clips.changeMeaning: The label shifts to the pulmonary valve between the right ventricle and pulmonary trunk, then to the aortic valve between the left ventricle and aorta. These semilunar valves are shown at the exit points of both ventricles.
clips.narration: The two semilunar valves guard the exits from the ventricles. The pulmonary valve sits between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk, allowing blood to exit to the lungs while preventing backflow. The aortic valve sits between the left ventricle and the aorta, allowing blood to exit to the body while preventing backflow. These valves will close during ventricular relaxation to prevent blood from returning.

clips.changeMeaning: The label moves to highlight the superior and inferior vena cava on both the cutaway and intact hearts. Lines or arrows show the direction of blood flow into the right atrium.
clips.narration: The major vessels complete the circuit. The superior and inferior vena cava return deoxygenated blood from the body into the right atrium. The superior vena cava brings blood from the upper body and head; the inferior vena cava brings blood from the lower body and organs. Together they carry the body's metabolic waste—carbon dioxide and depleted oxygen—back to the heart.

clips.changeMeaning: The label highlights the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries leaving the right ventricle, and the pulmonary veins returning to the left atrium. The color scheme may shift to show deoxygenated blood leaving and oxygenated blood returning.
clips.narration: The pulmonary circulation is a short loop dedicated to oxygenation. The pulmonary trunk exits the right ventricle and splits into left and right pulmonary arteries, carrying deoxygenated blood to the lungs. The pulmonary veins return the now-oxygenated blood to the left atrium. Note that pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood and pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood—the reverse of the systemic circulation.

clips.changeMeaning: The label highlights the aorta exiting the left ventricle, showing it as the main artery for systemic circulation. The cutaway and intact views both show the aorta's position at the top of the heart.
clips.narration: The aorta is the largest and thickest artery in the body. It receives oxygenated blood directly from the left ventricle and branches extensively to deliver blood to every region of the body—the head, the limbs, the organs, and the trunk. The ascending aorta branches first to the coronary arteries supplying the heart muscle itself. This completes our structural inventory: four chambers, four valves, and five major vessels.

modules.description: A dynamic visualization of blood flow through the pulmonary and systemic circuits, color-coded by oxygenation status.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish oxygenated blood (red) from deoxygenated blood (blue) by circuit
Recognize the pulmonary circuit as a short loop dedicated to oxygenation
Recognize the systemic circuit as a large loop delivering oxygen and nutrients throughout the body
Understand that both circuits operate simultaneously within a single heart

clips.changeMeaning: The chambers and vessels fill with flowing color: blue for deoxygenated blood on the right side, red for oxygenated blood on the left side. The flow appears smooth and continuous throughout the heart.
clips.narration: The heart drives two simultaneous circuits. On the right side of the heart, deoxygenated blood (shown in blue) is pumped to the lungs to be oxygenated. On the left side, oxygenated blood (shown in red) is pumped out to the body. The right and left sides are separated by the septum, a wall of tissue that prevents blood from mixing. Watch as the color shows the continuous, steady-state pattern of circulation.

clips.changeMeaning: The pulmonary circuit elements—right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, pulmonary valve, pulmonary arteries, and lungs—are highlighted with a distinct visual effect (glow, border, or emphasis). The blue deoxygenated flow is traced clearly through this loop.
clips.narration: Focus on the pulmonary circuit: deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium from the body, passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, is pumped through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and arteries, and travels to the lungs. In the lung capillaries, the blood releases carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen, becoming oxygenated. The pathway is brief and efficient because the lungs are located near the heart.

clips.changeMeaning: The systemic circuit elements—pulmonary veins, left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, and aorta—are highlighted. The red oxygenated flow is traced clearly through this large loop extending throughout the body.
clips.narration: Now focus on the systemic circuit: oxygenated blood returns from the lungs via the pulmonary veins into the left atrium, passes through the mitral valve into the left ventricle, is pumped powerfully through the aortic valve into the aorta, and distributes to every organ and tissue in the body. In the tissues, oxygen is consumed and carbon dioxide is produced, turning the blood blue. This deoxygenated blood is then returned to the right atrium by the venae cavae, completing the cycle.

modules.moduleName: Red Blood Cell Trace: Step-by-Step Journey
modules.description: An interactive journey following a single red blood cell through all chambers, valves, and vessels, emphasizing the sequence and function of each structure.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Recite the complete path of blood through the heart and lungs
Describe the functional role of each chamber and valve in advancing the blood cell
Understand gas exchange as the purpose of the pulmonary circuit

components.text: Click NEXT to advance the blood cell through the circulation.

clips.changeMeaning: A single large red blood cell appears in the superior vena cava, colored blue to indicate deoxygenation. The location label identifies the current position. The scene is paused, waiting for user input to advance.
clips.narration: A single red blood cell has just entered the superior vena cava. You will now step this cell through each stage of its journey. Pay attention to which chamber or vessel it enters, the function that chamber performs, and the valve it must pass through. Press NEXT to advance the cell to its first destination.

clips.changeMeaning: The red blood cell rapidly progresses through all major structures in sequence: right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, pulmonary valve, pulmonary arteries, lungs (where color changes to red), pulmonary veins, left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, aorta, then returns as blue through systemic circulation back to superior vena cava. Labels and brief narration accompany each major transition.
clips.narration: Watch as this red blood cell travels through the complete circulation pathway. It enters the right atrium from the superior vena cava, passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, is ejected through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary arteries, travels to the lungs where it becomes oxygenated and turns red, returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, passes through the mitral valve into the left ventricle, is powerfully ejected through the aortic valve into the aorta, distributes throughout the body, becomes deoxygenated through gas exchange in tissue capillaries, and returns to the starting point. This entire journey takes about one minute during rest.

clips.changeMeaning: The red blood cell returns to the superior vena cava, now colored blue again to show deoxygenation. The label updates to reflect completion of one cycle. The scene resets for replay.
clips.narration: One complete cycle is finished. The red blood cell is back in the superior vena cava, deoxygenated and ready to be pumped back to the lungs. In a living heart, this cycle repeats 60 to 100 times per minute at rest, and can accelerate to 150-200 times per minute during exercise. You can replay this trace as many times as you wish to reinforce the sequence. Press NEXT to view the trace again, or move to the next module.

modules.moduleName: Ventricular Wall Thickness and Functional Significance
modules.description: A comparison of right and left ventricular wall thickness, relating anatomical asymmetry to circulatory function and pressure requirements.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Measure and compare the thickness of the right and left ventricular myocardium
Understand that wall thickness reflects the pressure the ventricle must generate
Explain why the left ventricle requires a thicker wall than the right ventricle
Recognize the relationship between anatomical structure and physiological function

clips.changeMeaning: The scene displays cross-sectional views of both ventricles at the same horizontal level. The right ventricle on the left is highlighted with thin myocardium; the left ventricle on the right is highlighted with thick myocardium. Scale markers are visible to allow students to measure the difference.
clips.narration: Examine these two cross-sections of the heart, both cut at the same level through the ventricles. Notice immediately the dramatic difference in wall thickness. The right ventricle, on the left, has a thin myocardial wall—approximately 3 to 5 millimeters thick in a healthy adult. The left ventricle, on the right, has a much thicker wall—approximately 10 to 15 millimeters. This three-to-one thickness ratio is not random; it reflects a fundamental principle relating structure to function.

clips.changeMeaning: The images are annotated with pressure values or bars showing relative pressures in the pulmonary circuit (low) versus systemic circuit (high). The narration emphasizes the functional basis for the anatomical difference.
clips.narration: The left ventricle is thicker because it must generate much higher pressure to pump blood throughout the entire body against significant resistance. The systemic circulation extends to your fingertips, your toes, every organ—a vast network requiring substantial pressure to perfuse. The right ventricle, by contrast, only pumps to the lungs, which are located immediately adjacent to the heart and offer relatively low resistance. The pressures in the pulmonary circuit are about one-fifth those of the systemic circuit.

clips.changeMeaning: A note or label appears indicating that pathological conditions can alter wall thickness. The healthy thickness ratio is emphasized as a baseline for understanding disease states like left ventricular hypertrophy from chronic hypertension.
clips.narration: Understanding this asymmetry is clinically important. If blood pressure remains abnormally high for months or years, the left ventricle must work harder and may develop pathologically thick walls—a condition called left ventricular hypertrophy. Conversely, damage to the right ventricle from chronic lung disease can lead to its dilatation and dysfunction. By learning the normal structure-function relationships first, you will be better prepared to understand and explain these pathological changes in clinical contexts.

modules.moduleName: Valve Function and Prevention of Backflow
modules.description: An examination of how the four valves function to ensure one-way blood flow, categorizing them by location and mechanism.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Categorize valves as atrioventricular (AV) or semilunar valves based on location
Describe the mechanism by which each valve opens and closes
Explain the role of each valve in preventing backflow during different phases of the cardiac cycle
Relate valve structure to valve function

clips.changeMeaning: The cutaway heart is displayed with all four valves highlighted in two categories: AV valves (tricuspid and mitral) in one color, semilunar valves (pulmonary and aortic) in another. Text labels clearly mark the two categories.
clips.narration: The heart's four valves fall into two functional categories based on their location and purpose. The atrioventricular valves sit between the atria and ventricles: these are the tricuspid valve on the right and the mitral valve on the left. The semilunar valves sit between the ventricles and their outflow arteries: these are the pulmonary valve on the right and the aortic valve on the left. Each category has different structural features that suit its function.

clips.changeMeaning: A large-scale model of an atrioventricular valve appears on the left, showing the valve in two states: open (leaflets splayed apart) and closed (leaflets together). The models alternate to show the transition. Text describes the mechanism of opening and closing.
clips.narration: Atrioventricular valves have two or three leaflets attached at their base to a fibrous ring. When the atrium contracts, blood pressure pushes the leaflets open, allowing blood to flow into the ventricle below. When the ventricle contracts, ventricular pressure pushes the leaflets upward, sealing the opening and preventing backflow into the atrium. This is a passive mechanism—the leaflets respond to pressure changes without any active muscular control. The tricuspid valve has three leaflets; the mitral valve has two.

clips.changeMeaning: A large-scale model of a semilunar valve appears on the right, showing the valve in two states: open (leaflets cupped downward) and closed (leaflets pushed up, forming a cone). The models alternate to show the transition. The distinct architecture is highlighted.
clips.narration: Semilunar valves have three leaflets arranged in a cup-like pattern, shaped like three half-moons facing each other. When the ventricle contracts, blood pressure pushes these leaflets apart and out of the way, allowing blood to flow into the artery. When the ventricle relaxes, blood pressure in the artery—which is now higher than in the ventricle—fills the cup-shaped pockets of the leaflets, pushing them together and sealing the valve. Again, this is a passive, pressure-driven mechanism. The key difference from AV valves is the cup-shaped design, which seals effectively even under high arterial pressure.

clips.changeMeaning: The cutaway heart animates the cardiac cycle, showing both systole and diastole phases. During systole, AV valves are closed (highlighted red) and semilunar valves are open (highlighted green). During diastole, the pattern reverses.
clips.narration: During ventricular contraction—systole—the atrioventricular valves are firmly closed, preventing blood from being pushed backward into the atria. Simultaneously, the semilunar valves are wide open, allowing the ventricles to eject blood into the arteries. During ventricular relaxation—diastole—the atrioventricular valves open, allowing blood to flow from the atria into the ventricles. The semilunar valves are now tightly closed, preventing blood in the arteries from flowing backward into the relaxing ventricles. This alternating pattern, driven entirely by pressure changes, ensures one-way flow of blood through the heart.

modules.description: Short quizzes testing identification of structures and blood flow sequences, followed by a comprehensive recap of all major concepts.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Accurately identify the four chambers, four valves, and major vessels by name
Sequence the chambers and vessels in the correct order of blood flow
Synthesize all major concept areas into a coherent understanding of cardiac anatomy and function

components.text:
Structural Inventory: 4 Chambers, 4 Valves, 5 Vessels
Dual-Circuit Organization: Pulmonary + Systemic
Blood Path: Complete circuit in ~1 minute
Wall Thickness: LV (10-15 mm) >> RV (3-5 mm)
Valve Function: One-way flow, prevention of backflow

clips.changeMeaning: The quiz mode is introduced. The cutaway heart is displayed with all labels hidden. The first structure is highlighted with a glow. Multiple-choice answer options appear. The scene is ready for user interaction.
clips.narration: You will now take a short quiz to test your ability to identify heart structures by sight and trace the path of blood through the circulation. A structure will be highlighted, and you will select the correct name from multiple options. Let's begin. Remember to use both the internal anatomy from the cutaway view and the external landmarks from the intact heart to guide your answers.

clips.changeMeaning: The quiz progresses through identification of the four chambers, four valves, and five major vessels in random order. After each answer, brief feedback confirms correctness or provides correction. Highlighted regions on the heart correspond to each structure. The quiz then transitions to blood flow questions: 'Blood is in the right atrium. What is the next structure?' with multiple-choice options.
clips.narration: Select the correct answer for each highlighted structure or blood flow scenario. If you are uncertain, take time to review the structure. After completing all questions, you will receive a summary of your performance and recommendations for further study.

clips.changeMeaning: The quiz concludes and transitions to a recap screen. All five major concept areas are listed with brief summaries. The cutaway heart appears beneath with all structures visible, color-coded by circuit or functional category.
clips.narration: Excellent work! You have completed the cardiac anatomy lab. Let's review the five major concepts: the structural inventory of four chambers, four valves, and five major vessels; the dual-circuit organization of pulmonary and systemic circulation; the complete path of blood through the circuits in approximately one minute; the wall thickness asymmetry of left and right ventricles reflecting their different circulatory loads; and the function of atrioventricular and semilunar valves in maintaining one-way blood flow. You now have a comprehensive foundation for understanding cardiac physiology, pathology, and clinical assessment. Congratulations on completing this laboratory!
